name: odin
desc: Programming language with focus on simplicity, performance and modern systems
why: A systems language with a distinctive design philosophy that is worth an afternoon for anyone who has not tried it.

brief.what_it_is: Odin is a general-purpose, open source compiled programming language with distinct typing, aimed at high performance and modern systems. The source code you write goes to the Odin compiler, which produces native programs. The language ships with a core library of packages (fmt, simd and others) and a vendor library of official bindings for graphics APIs and libraries such as SDL2, GLFW, raylib, microui and miniaudio. The homepage's showcase lists many programs and Steam games written in it.
brief.why_it_exists: The README calls Odin 'the C alternative for the joy of programming' and 'The Data-Oriented Language for Sane Software Development'. The homepage's stated principles are simplicity ('clear is better than clever'), high performance through low-level control of memory layout and custom allocators, and built-in support for modern hardware such as SOA data types and array programming.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage examples show the language's built-in features rather than a single mechanism: fixed and slice arrays with component-wise array math and swizzles, bit_set and enumerated arrays, defer for cleanup at scope exit, multiple return values, labelled control flow, SIMD vectors and inline assembly. The README does not describe the compiler's internals.
brief.install_notes: The homepage links to a Getting Started install page (https://odin-lang.org/docs/install) and a nightly builds page, which I did not fetch, so I cannot give the exact steps beyond the brew formula. The README and homepage mention no accounts, runtimes or hardware requirements. Programs are written in .odin files with a 'package main' and a 'main :: proc()' entry point, and the homepage examples import 'core:fmt'. The brew formula installs the 'odin' executable.
brief.standout: Odin takes a data-oriented route: bit sets, enumerated arrays, SOA layout, SIMD and built-in array programming are part of the language, not libraries. Its batteries-included approach (official graphics bindings for Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D and WebGL, plus raylib and SDL bindings) is unusual for a young language, and the homepage shows a long list of games shipped on Steam built with it.
brief.status: Active as far as I can tell, though the README gives no release date. The GitHub README I fetched includes a release badge linking to the latest release, a CI badge and a Discord badge, and the homepage lists current Steam releases and an active nightly builds page. I could not confirm a last-release or last-commit date from these pages, so the exact date is unknown.
brief.caveats: The README's own warning says 'The Odin compiler is still in development.' The compiler's platforms, per the README badge, are Windows, Linux and macOS. The homepage's showcase is marketing-heavy and includes many commercial products. I did not check the license file, though the homepage calls Odin open source. The brew caveats field is empty.
quotes: Odin is the C alternative for the Joy of Programming.
Simplicity is complicated to get right, clear is better than clever.
The Odin compiler is still in development.
